quotes.text: The uncomfortable truth is that patchwork debugging doesn't just slow things down, It reinforces a culture of reaction instead of design.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Names the cultural cost of reactive debugging, not just the time cost.

quotes.text: This is not about replacing your judgment. It's about removing the repetitive bookkeeping so you can focus on the actual design choices.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clarifies the intended role of agent mode as an assistant rather than a replacement.

quotes.text: It's worth stressing agents can help move faster, but they don't replace good engineering practices. You should still treat code reviews and CI as non negotiable gatekeepers.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: With agent support, you outline the idea in natural words, the scaffold shows up and you can iterate almost as quickly as vibe coding, while keeping the benefit of an organized structure.

quotes.text: Offloading repetitive setup doesn't weaken your expertise, it preserves it for design and architecture, where judgment creates leverage.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

From error hunts to autonomous fixes

takeaways: GitHub Copilot's agent mode holds context across multiple files, so a change such as a new Azure Function can include the method, bindings, host.json and dependency registration in one coordinated step.
A plain-language spec can be turned into a scaffold of controllers, models and service registrations, giving a middle ground between vibe coding and heavy spec-first design.
Agents reduce cross-file friction, but you still review the diff, run unit tests and CI and decide what gets merged.
hook: .NET and Azure developers lose whole afternoons to code-compile-error loops and config drift across many files. This episode shows how GitHub Copilot's agent mode coordinates multi-file changes, fixes cross-file errors and scaffolds features from a plain-language spec, while you keep control through review and CI.
